questions.q: What does a single artificial neuron in a fully connected layer compute?
options: The maximum of its inputs passed through a softmax
A weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation function
The average of its inputs multiplied by a learned scalar
A lookup of its input index in a learned table
questions.why: A neuron computes z = w·x + b and then applies a (usually nonlinear) activation such as ReLU. Max-pooling and softmax are separate operations, and a table lookup describes an embedding layer, not a neuron.

questions.q: A developer builds a 10-layer network but forgets to add activation functions between the linear layers. What is the consequence?
options: The network trains faster and generalizes better
The network can only output values between 0 and 1
Gradients explode on the first backward pass
The whole stack is equivalent to a single linear transformation
questions.why: A composition of linear (affine) maps is itself affine, so depth adds no expressive power without nonlinear activations. Output range is not restricted to (0,1) unless a sigmoid is applied, and exploding gradients are not an automatic result of missing activations.

questions.q: Which function defines the ReLU activation?
options: f(x) = max(0, x)
f(x) = x · Φ(x)
questions.why: ReLU passes positive inputs unchanged and zeroes negative ones, which makes it cheap and avoids saturation for positive values. Option C is GELU (x times the Gaussian CDF), B is sigmoid and D is tanh.

questions.q: An engineer needs a single output that can be read as the probability of a binary label. Which activation produces outputs strictly in the range (0, 1)?
options: ReLU
tanh
Sigmoid
Leaky ReLU
questions.why: The logistic sigmoid squashes any real input into (0, 1), which is why it is used for binary probabilities and inside LSTM gates. tanh is tempting but its range is (−1, 1), and ReLU/Leaky ReLU are unbounded above.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of tanh over sigmoid as a hidden-layer activation?
options: It never saturates for large inputs
It has no gradient for negative inputs
Its output is zero-centered in the range (−1, 1)
It is cheaper to compute than ReLU
questions.why: Zero-centered outputs make downstream gradient updates better balanced than sigmoid's all-positive outputs. tanh still saturates at large |x|, so it does not solve vanishing gradients, and it is more expensive than ReLU.

questions.q: Which activation function is used in the feed-forward layers of the original BERT and GPT-2 models?
options: GELU
Sigmoid
tanh
Softplus
questions.why: BERT and GPT-2 use GELU, a smooth ReLU-like function that weights inputs by the Gaussian CDF. Sigmoid and tanh saturate and are rarely used in transformer FFNs; softplus is smooth but was not the choice in these models.

questions.q: The LLaMA family of models replaced the standard ReLU/GELU feed-forward layer with which variant?
options: Maxout
ELU
Leaky ReLU
SwiGLU
questions.why: SwiGLU is a gated linear unit that multiplies a Swish (SiLU)-activated projection elementwise with a second linear projection, and it improved quality in PaLM and LLaMA. Leaky ReLU and ELU are ungated activations and do not add the extra gating projection.

questions.q: A deep network trained with sigmoid activations shows early layers whose weights barely change. What is the most likely cause?
options: Exploding gradients
Vanishing gradients
Overfitting
A learning rate that is too high
questions.why: Backpropagation multiplies many small sigmoid derivatives together, so gradients reaching early layers shrink toward zero and those layers stop learning. Exploding gradients would produce huge, unstable updates rather than frozen early layers.

questions.q: A 32×32 single-channel image passes through a 5×5 convolution with stride 1 and no padding. What is the spatial size of the output?
questions.why: Output size = (N − K + 2P) / S + 1 = (32 − 5 + 0) / 1 + 1 = 28. Keeping 32×32 would require "same" padding of 2 pixels per side, and 27 is the off-by-one result of forgetting the +1.

questions.q: What does a residual (skip) connection do in a transformer block?
options: Skips the block entirely during inference to save compute
Multiplies the block output by its input
Concatenates the input and output along the feature dimension
Adds the block's input to its output so gradients have a direct path
questions.why: A residual connection computes y = x + F(x), giving an identity path that lets gradients flow through very deep stacks. It is addition, not concatenation (as in DenseNet), and the block is still executed at inference.

questions.q: Over which dimension does Layer Normalization compute its mean and variance in a transformer?
options: Across the hidden (feature) dimension of each individual token
Across the batch dimension for each feature
Across all tokens in the sequence for each feature
Across all parameters of the layer
questions.why: LayerNorm normalizes each token vector using statistics over its own features, so it is independent of batch size and sequence length. Normalizing over the batch for each feature is BatchNorm.

questions.q: Why do transformers use LayerNorm rather than BatchNorm?
options: BatchNorm has no learnable parameters
LayerNorm removes the need for residual connections
LayerNorm does not depend on batch statistics, which are unreliable with variable-length sequences and small batches
BatchNorm cannot be used on GPUs
questions.why: BatchNorm's statistics are noisy with small batches and awkward with padding, and they behave differently in training and inference. BatchNorm does have learnable scale and shift parameters, so A is false.

questions.q: How does RMSNorm differ from LayerNorm?
options: It normalizes across the batch instead of the features
It adds a learned positional bias
It skips mean subtraction and scales only by the root mean square
It is applied only to the attention scores
questions.why: RMSNorm divides by sqrt(mean(x²) + ε) and applies a learned gain, dropping re-centering and the bias term, which is slightly cheaper with similar quality. It still normalizes per token over features, not across the batch.

questions.q: A team notices that a large fraction of ReLU units output zero for every training example and never recover. What is this problem called?
options: Dying ReLU
Mode collapse
Covariate shift
Saturation of the softmax
questions.why: If a ReLU unit's pre-activation is always negative, its output and gradient are both zero, so the unit can no longer learn. Mode collapse is a GAN failure where the generator produces limited variety, not a neuron-level issue.

questions.q: What distinguishes a recurrent neural network (RNN) from a feed-forward network?
options: It uses convolutions to share weights across space
It attends to all positions in parallel
It has no trainable parameters in the hidden layer
It carries a hidden state that is updated step by step through the sequence
questions.why: An RNN applies the same weights at each time step and passes a hidden state forward, giving it memory of earlier inputs. Attending to all positions in parallel describes self-attention, which is exactly what RNNs lack.

questions.q: Which set of gates is found in a standard LSTM cell?
options: Query, key and value gates
Forget, input and output gates
Update and reset gates
Encoder and decoder gates
questions.why: The LSTM uses forget, input and output gates to control what enters, stays in and leaves its cell state. Update and reset gates belong to the GRU, a simplified variant.

questions.q: Compared with an LSTM, a GRU:
options: Has more gates and a separate cell state
Merges cell and hidden state and uses two gates, so it has fewer parameters
Cannot model long-range dependencies at all
Requires attention to function
questions.why: The GRU uses update and reset gates and a single hidden state, making it lighter than the three-gate LSTM. It still mitigates vanishing gradients reasonably well, so C overstates its limits.

questions.q: What is the main reason transformers displaced RNNs for large-scale language modeling?
options: Transformers use fewer parameters per layer
Transformers do not need positional information
RNNs cannot be trained with backpropagation
Transformers process all positions of a sequence in parallel during training
questions.why: RNNs must compute step t after step t−1, which limits GPU utilization; self-attention handles all positions at once and links distant tokens in one step. Transformers actually need explicit positional information because attention is order-agnostic, so B is wrong.

questions.q: What property makes convolutional layers efficient for images?
options: Local receptive fields with weights shared across spatial positions
Every output pixel connects to every input pixel with unique weights
They process pixels sequentially like an RNN
They require no training
questions.why: A small kernel slides over the image and reuses the same weights everywhere, giving translation equivariance and far fewer parameters than a dense layer. Option B describes a fully connected layer.

questions.q: In an early RNN encoder–decoder for translation without attention, what limited quality on long sentences?
options: The decoder could not generate more than one token
The vocabulary was too large for the softmax
The whole source sentence was compressed into one fixed-length vector
The encoder used convolutions
questions.why: The decoder only saw the encoder's final hidden state, a bottleneck that lost information as sentences grew. Attention fixed this by letting the decoder look at all encoder states at every step.

questions.q: Which expression is scaled dot-product attention?
options: softmax(QV^T / d_k) K
softmax(Q + K) V
softmax(QK^T / √d_k) V
sigmoid(QK^T) V / √d_k
questions.why: Queries are compared with keys by dot product, scaled by √d_k, normalized with softmax, and used to take a weighted sum of values. Option D applies sigmoid and scales after weighting, which does not produce a normalized distribution over positions.

questions.q: Why are attention scores divided by √d_k?
options: Large dot products push softmax into saturated regions with tiny gradients
It converts the scores into probabilities
It removes the need for a causal mask
It reduces the memory needed for the attention matrix
questions.why: With unit-variance components, the dot product of two d_k-dimensional vectors has variance d_k, so scores grow with dimension and softmax becomes nearly one-hot. Scaling restores unit variance; softmax, not the scaling, turns scores into probabilities.

questions.q: In self-attention, what role does the query vector of a token play?
options: It holds the content that is copied into the output
It encodes the token's absolute position
It stores the normalization statistics for the layer
It is compared against every key to decide how much to attend to each position
questions.why: The query represents what the token is looking for; its dot products with keys produce the attention weights. The content that is mixed into the output comes from the value vectors, not the query.

questions.q: A decoder-only model is trained on next-token prediction. Why is a causal mask applied to the attention scores?
options: To ignore padding tokens in the batch
To stop each position from attending to tokens that come after it
To reduce the number of attention heads
To make attention bidirectional
questions.why: Without the mask, a position could see the very token it is supposed to predict, leaking the answer during training. Ignoring padding is the job of a separate padding mask.

questions.q: In *self*-attention, where do the queries, keys and values come from?
options: Queries from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder
Keys from the input, queries and values from learned constants
All three are linear projections of the same input sequence
Values from the positional encoding only
questions.why: Self-attention projects one sequence with three learned matrices W_Q, W_K, W_V, so tokens attend to each other within that sequence. Taking queries from the decoder and keys/values from the encoder is cross-attention.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of multi-head attention over a single attention head of the same total width?
options: It removes the need for the feed-forward network
It makes attention complexity linear in sequence length
It guarantees that each head attends only to adjacent tokens
Different heads can attend to different relationships in separate subspaces
questions.why: Each head has its own projections, so one may track syntax while another tracks coreference, and their outputs are concatenated and projected. The quadratic cost in sequence length is unchanged by splitting into heads.

questions.q: A transformer has d_model = 768 and 12 attention heads. What is the dimension of each head's query vector?
questions.why: Standard multi-head attention splits d_model evenly: 768 / 12 = 64 per head. 768 would be the full model width, and 9,216 (768 × 12) wrongly multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.q: Why do transformers need positional encodings?
options: To reduce the vocabulary size
To normalize the embeddings
Self-attention by itself is permutation-equivariant and ignores token order
To allow the model to use a causal mask
questions.why: Shuffling the input tokens just shuffles the attention outputs, so "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look the same without positional signals. The causal mask works independently of positional encodings.

questions.q: How did the original "Attention Is All You Need" transformer encode token positions?
options: Rotary embeddings applied to queries and keys
A linear bias on attention scores
Fixed sine and cosine functions of different frequencies added to the embeddings
A learned embedding per position only
questions.why: The original paper added deterministic sinusoids with geometrically spaced wavelengths to the token embeddings. The authors also tried learned position embeddings with similar results, but the reported design used sinusoids; RoPE and ALiBi came later.

questions.q: Which description fits BERT?
options: Encoder-only model pretrained with masked language modeling
Decoder-only model pretrained on next-token prediction
Encoder–decoder model trained on text-to-text tasks
Recurrent model trained with teacher forcing
questions.why: BERT stacks transformer encoders and learns by predicting randomly masked tokens using context from both sides. Decoder-only next-token prediction describes GPT, and text-to-text encoder–decoder describes T5.

questions.q: What architecture and objective does the GPT family use?
options: Encoder-only with masked token prediction
Encoder–decoder with span corruption
Convolutional with contrastive loss
Decoder-only with causal (next-token) language modeling
questions.why: GPT models use a stack of causally masked transformer blocks trained to predict the next token. Span corruption with an encoder–decoder is T5's pretraining objective.

questions.q: What is distinctive about T5's framing of NLP tasks?
options: It uses only an encoder and a classification head
It casts every task as text-to-text with an encoder–decoder model
It removes attention in favor of recurrence
It predicts only the next token with no encoder
questions.why: T5 turns translation, classification and summarization alike into "input text → output text" with a task prefix. An encoder plus classification head is the usual BERT setup.

questions.q: What does the position-wise feed-forward network in a standard transformer block consist of?
options: A single attention head with a larger dimension
Two linear layers with a nonlinearity, applied independently to each token
A recurrent layer over the sequence
A convolution across neighboring tokens
questions.why: The FFN expands to a hidden size (typically 4 × d_model), applies an activation, and projects back, with the same weights at every position. It does not mix information across tokens; that is attention's job.

questions.q: Which 2017 paper introduced the transformer architecture?
options: "BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers"
"Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks"
"Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition"
"Attention Is All You Need"
questions.why: Vaswani et al. (2017) proposed a model built entirely on attention and feed-forward layers, dropping recurrence. BERT (2018) built on the transformer encoder, and the seq2seq paper used LSTMs.

questions.q: What is the token embedding layer of an LLM, in implementation terms?
options: A learned matrix of shape (vocab_size, d_model) indexed by token ID
A fixed one-hot encoding of each token
A convolution over characters
A hash function computed at runtime
questions.why: `nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)` stores one trainable dense vector per token and simply looks up rows by ID. One-hot vectors are sparse and not learned; the embedding is equivalent to multiplying a one-hot vector by this matrix.

questions.q: What does "weight tying" mean in a language model?
options: Sharing the same weights across all transformer layers
Freezing the embedding layer during training
Using the input embedding matrix (transposed) as the output projection to vocabulary logits
Forcing all attention heads to have identical weights
questions.why: Tying reuses the vocab × d_model embedding for the LM head, saving parameters and often improving quality, as in GPT-2. Sharing weights across all layers is a different technique (used in ALBERT).

questions.q: How does the compute and memory of standard self-attention scale with sequence length n?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n²)
O(n³)
questions.why: Every token's query is compared against every key, producing an n × n score matrix per head. The linear O(n) behavior belongs to the per-token feed-forward layers, which is why attention dominates at long context.

questions.q: After softmax, what is true of each row of the attention weight matrix?
options: It sums to 1
It contains only 0s and 1s
It sums to √d_k
It is always symmetric with its column
questions.why: Softmax is applied over the key dimension, turning each query's scores into a probability distribution over positions. Weights are soft (not binary), and the matrix is generally not symmetric because Q and K use different projections.

questions.q: A data scientist needs to classify support tickets into categories and extract entity names. Which architecture family is most naturally suited?
options: Diffusion model
GAN
Decoder-only causal LM with no fine-tuning
Encoder-only model such as BERT
questions.why: Encoders see the full context in both directions and produce rich per-token and sequence representations, ideal for classification and NER. Decoder-only models can do it with prompting, but they only see left context per token and are usually larger and costlier for this job.

questions.q: In a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) transformer layer, what does the router (gating network) do?
options: Chooses which GPU the whole model runs on
Sends each token to a small subset of expert feed-forward networks
Averages the outputs of all experts equally for every token
Decides the order of transformer layers
questions.why: The router scores the experts per token and activates only the top-k, so total parameters grow while per-token compute stays modest. Averaging all experts for every token would be a dense model with no compute savings.

questions.q: What do neural scaling laws (e.g., Kaplan et al., 2020) describe?
options: How GPU clock speed scales with temperature
Test loss decreasing as a power law in model size, data and compute
Accuracy growing linearly with the number of attention heads
The maximum sequence length a model can support
questions.why: Language-model loss falls predictably as a power law when parameters, tokens or compute are scaled, as long as the others are not bottlenecks. The relationship is a smooth power law, not linear in a single architectural hyperparameter like head count.

questions.q: The Chinchilla study found that compute-optimal training uses roughly how many training tokens per model parameter?
questions.why: Hoffmann et al. (2022) found parameters and tokens should grow in equal proportion, which works out to about 20 tokens per parameter. Earlier large models like GPT-3 (~1.7 tokens per parameter) were undertrained by that standard.

questions.q: Why does a convolutional layer need far fewer parameters than a fully connected layer applied to the same image?
options: The same small kernel weights are reused at every spatial position
Convolutions process only the color channels, not individual pixels
Pooling layers store the weights instead of the convolution
Convolutional layers have no bias terms
questions.why: A convolution slides one small kernel across the image, sharing its parameters across all positions, which also makes the layer translation-equivariant. Pooling layers have no learned weights, so they cannot hold the parameters.

questions.q: Besides the reconstruction loss, what term does a Variational Autoencoder's training objective include?
options: An adversarial loss from a discriminator
A contrastive loss between image and text pairs
A KL divergence pulling the latent distribution toward a prior
A next-token cross-entropy loss
questions.why: The VAE maximizes the ELBO: reconstruct the input well while keeping the encoder's latent distribution close to a standard normal prior, which makes the latent space smooth enough to sample from. Adversarial losses belong to GANs, not plain VAEs.

questions.q: How does a diffusion model generate an image?
options: In a single forward pass from a random latent, judged by a discriminator
By predicting pixels one at a time left to right
By starting from pure noise and iteratively denoising it with a learned network
By retrieving the nearest training image
questions.why: Training teaches a network to undo a gradual noising process; sampling runs that reversal over many steps. Single-pass generation with a discriminator describes a GAN, and pixel-by-pixel prediction describes autoregressive image models.

questions.q: How does a Vision Transformer (ViT) turn an image into transformer input?
options: It splits the image into fixed-size patches and linearly embeds each patch as a token
It feeds each pixel as a separate token
It converts the image to a caption first
It runs an LSTM over image rows
questions.why: ViT cuts the image into patches (e.g., 16×16), flattens and projects each one, adds position embeddings and a class token. Per-pixel tokens would make the sequence enormous and attention prohibitively expensive.

questions.q: How is CLIP trained?
options: Masked image modeling on unlabeled photos
Next-token prediction on image captions only
Denoising image latents conditioned on text
Contrastive learning that aligns image and text embeddings of matching pairs
questions.why: CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder so matching pairs have high cosine similarity and mismatched pairs low. Denoising latents conditioned on text describes a text-to-image diffusion model, which often uses a CLIP-style text encoder but is a different model.

questions.q: What does the final layer of a decoder-only LLM produce at each position?
options: A single scalar reward
A vector of logits over the vocabulary, turned into probabilities by softmax
The next token's embedding vector directly
A binary mask over the context
questions.why: The LM head projects the final hidden state to vocab_size logits, and softmax gives a next-token distribution. Predicting an embedding vector directly is not how standard LMs work, and a scalar output is what a reward model produces.

questions.q: Which network is trained to reconstruct its own input after passing it through a lower-dimensional bottleneck, yielding a compressed representation?
options: A generative adversarial network
An autoencoder
A recurrent neural network
A gradient-boosted tree ensemble
questions.why: An autoencoder's encoder compresses the input into a latent code and its decoder reconstructs the input, trained with a reconstruction loss. A GAN learns to generate samples by competing with a discriminator and never reconstructs a given input.

questions.q: Which initialization is designed for layers followed by ReLU activations?
options: All weights set to zero
Xavier/Glorot initialization
All weights set to one
He (Kaiming) initialization
questions.why: He init uses variance 2/fan_in to compensate for ReLU zeroing half the inputs, keeping activation variance stable across layers. Xavier targets symmetric activations like tanh, and constant initialization makes all neurons identical (symmetry is never broken).

questions.q: Where do most modern LLMs (GPT-2 onward, LLaMA) place layer normalization relative to each sublayer?
options: Before the sublayer, inside the residual branch (pre-norm)
After the residual addition (post-norm)
Only once at the input embedding
Only on the attention scores
questions.why: Pre-norm computes x + F(Norm(x)), leaving a clean identity path that makes deep models train more stably. The original 2017 transformer used post-norm, Norm(x + F(x)), which is harder to train at depth.

questions.q: Which sequence matches one block of a pre-norm decoder-only transformer?
options: FFN → masked self-attention → norm → residual
Cross-attention → norm → FFN
Norm → masked self-attention → residual add → norm → FFN → residual add
Masked self-attention → softmax over vocabulary → FFN
questions.why: Each block has two sublayers, attention then FFN, each wrapped with a norm and a residual connection. Cross-attention appears only in encoder–decoder decoders, and the vocabulary softmax is applied once at the top of the model, not per block.

questions.q: How many trainable parameters does `nn.Linear(768, 3072)` have (bias enabled)?
questions.why: The weight matrix has 768 × 3072 = 2,359,296 entries and the bias adds one per output feature (3,072), for 2,362,368. Option A forgets the bias, and B adds a bias of size 768 (the input size) instead of the output size.

questions.q: Queries and keys have shape (batch=2, heads=8, seq=512, head_dim=64). What is the shape of `q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)`?
questions.why: Multiplying (…, 512, 64) by (…, 64, 512) gives one score per query–key pair: a 512 × 512 matrix per head per batch item. (2, 8, 512, 64) is the shape after multiplying the weights by V, not the score matrix.

questions.q: For one layer with 32 heads, batch size 1 and sequence length 4,096, how much memory does materializing the full attention score matrix in FP16 require?
options: 32 MiB
128 MiB
512 MiB
1 GiB
questions.why: 4,096² = 16.8M scores per head × 32 heads = 536.9M scores × 2 bytes = 1,073,741,824 bytes = 1 GiB. That is for a single layer, which is why kernels such as FlashAttention avoid storing this matrix at all.

questions.q: Ignoring biases and norms, a standard transformer block with model width d and a 4d FFN has approximately how many parameters?
options: 4d²
12d²
8d²
16d²
questions.why: Attention has four d × d matrices (Q, K, V, output) = 4d², and the FFN has d × 4d plus 4d × d = 8d², totaling 12d². 4d² counts only attention and 8d² only the FFN.

questions.q: Using the 12·L·d² approximation, about how many non-embedding parameters does a 24-layer transformer with d_model = 1,024 have?
questions.why: 12 × 24 × 1,024² = 12 × 24 × 1,048,576 ≈ 302M. This matches BERT-large's ~340M total once its embeddings are added; 101M would come from using 4d² per layer instead of 12d².

questions.q: GPT-2 small has a vocabulary of 50,257 tokens and d_model = 768. Approximately how many parameters are in its token embedding matrix?
questions.why: 50,257 × 768 ≈ 38.6M parameters, roughly a third of GPT-2 small's 124M total. Because GPT-2 ties its LM head to this matrix, the output projection adds no further parameters.

questions.q: A model has a 32,000-token vocabulary and d_model = 4,096, with untied input embedding and LM head. How many parameters do these two matrices hold together?
questions.why: Each matrix is 32,000 × 4,096 ≈ 131M, and untied means two separate copies: ≈ 262M. 131M would be correct only if the weights were tied.

questions.q:
What does this snippet do to the attention scores (shape T × T)?

```python
mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=1)
scores = scores.masked_fill(mask, float('-inf'))
weights = scores.softmax(dim=-1)
```
options: Hides each token from itself
Blocks attention to padding tokens
Gives zero weight to all keys at future positions
Gives zero weight to all keys at past positions
questions.why: `triu(..., diagonal=1)` is True strictly above the diagonal, i.e., where key index > query index; setting those to −inf makes softmax assign them zero weight. The diagonal is kept, so tokens still attend to themselves.

questions.q: In multi-head attention, `weights` has shape (B, H, T, T) and `v` has shape (B, H, T, 64). After `out = weights @ v`, which operation typically follows before the output projection?
options: Softmax over the last dimension
Transposing and reshaping to (B, T, H·64) to concatenate the heads
Applying the causal mask again
Averaging over the head dimension
questions.why: Head outputs (B, H, T, 64) are transposed to (B, T, H, 64) and flattened to (B, T, H·64) = (B, T, d_model), then passed through W_O. Heads are concatenated, not averaged, so each keeps its own subspace.

questions.q: What does Multi-Query Attention (MQA) change compared with standard multi-head attention?
options: All query heads share a single key head and a single value head
Each head gets its own separate feed-forward network
Queries are computed only for the last token
Attention is computed over multiple queries concatenated into one vector
questions.why: MQA keeps many query heads but uses one K and one V projection, shrinking the K/V tensors that must be stored and read during generation. It can cost some quality, which motivated the middle-ground GQA.

questions.q: A model uses 32 query heads and grouped-query attention with 8 key/value heads. How many query heads share each key/value head?
questions.why: 32 query heads ÷ 8 KV heads = 4 query heads per group. GQA with 1 KV head would be MQA, and with 32 KV heads it would be ordinary MHA.

questions.q: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is applied to which tensors?
options: The input token embeddings before the first layer
The query and key vectors in every attention layer
The value vectors only
The final logits
questions.why: RoPE rotates pairs of dimensions of Q and K by angles proportional to position, so position enters through the QK dot product. Unlike sinusoidal or learned encodings, nothing is added to the input embeddings, and values are not rotated.

questions.q: How does ALiBi (Attention with Linear Biases) encode position?
options: By concatenating a position index to each embedding
By adding a penalty proportional to query–key distance to the attention scores
By rotating queries and keys
By learning one embedding per absolute position
questions.why: ALiBi uses no position embeddings; it subtracts a head-specific slope × distance from each score, biasing attention toward nearby tokens. This helps models extrapolate to sequences longer than those seen in training.

questions.q: BERT uses learned absolute position embeddings for 512 positions. What happens if you need to feed it 1,024 tokens?
options: It works automatically because attention is length-agnostic
Positions beyond 512 reuse position 512's embedding with no issue
The model switches to relative positions
There are no trained embeddings for positions 513+, so the input must be truncated or the model extended and retrained
questions.why: A learned position table has exactly as many rows as max positions, so longer inputs index past the end. This hard limit is one reason relative schemes such as RoPE and ALiBi became popular.

questions.q: What is the maximum value of the derivative of the sigmoid function?
questions.why: σ'(x) = σ(x)(1 − σ(x)), which peaks at x = 0 where σ = 0.5, giving 0.25. Because it is always ≤ 0.25, chaining many sigmoids shrinks gradients; ReLU's derivative of 1 for positive inputs avoids this.

questions.q: If each of 10 stacked sigmoid layers contributes its maximum derivative (and weights are ≈ 1), roughly what factor scales the gradient reaching the first layer?
options: About 1 × 10⁻⁶
About 1 × 10⁻²⁰
questions.why: 0.25¹⁰ ≈ 9.5 × 10⁻⁷, so even in the best case the gradient shrinks about a millionfold. Option B wrongly multiplies 0.25 by 0.1 instead of raising it to the 10th power.

questions.q: An engineer trains a 48-layer post-norm transformer and the loss diverges early, while a 12-layer version trains fine. Which architectural change most directly improves stability?
options: Replace GELU with sigmoid
Remove the residual connections
Move to a pre-norm layout
Increase d_model without other changes
questions.why: Pre-norm keeps an un-normalized identity path from input to output, giving well-behaved gradients at depth, which is why GPT-2 and later LLMs adopted it. Removing residuals would make deep training much worse, not better.

questions.q: Why is BatchNorm a poor fit for autoregressive LLM inference with batch size 1?
options: It has no learnable parameters
It increases attention complexity
It requires a causal mask
It depends on batch statistics, which are meaningless at batch size 1 and must be replaced by running averages that may not match the data
questions.why: BatchNorm normalizes using statistics across examples, so its train-time and inference-time behavior differ and small batches are noisy. LayerNorm and RMSNorm compute per token and behave the same at any batch size.

questions.q: Which formula matches RMSNorm with learned gain g?
options: (x − mean(x)) / std(x) · g + b
x / max(|x|) · g
x / ‖x‖₁ · g
x / √(mean(x²) + ε) · g
questions.why: RMSNorm divides by the root mean square of the features with no mean subtraction and no bias. Option A is LayerNorm.

questions.q: Why does a SwiGLU feed-forward block typically use a hidden size of about (8/3)·d instead of 4d?
options: SiLU outputs are half the magnitude of ReLU outputs
It has three weight matrices instead of two, so the hidden size is reduced to keep parameter count similar
GQA requires a smaller FFN
The gate removes the need for a down projection
questions.why: SwiGLU computes (SiLU(xW₁) ⊙ xW₃)W₂: three d × h matrices give 3dh, and h = 8d/3 makes that 8d², matching a standard 4d FFN. It still needs the down projection W₂.

questions.q: A SwiGLU FFN has d_model = 4,096 and hidden size 11,008 with no biases. How many parameters does it contain?
questions.why: Each of the three matrices (gate, up, down) holds 4,096 × 11,008 ≈ 45.1M parameters, so the total is ≈ 135.3M. 90M would count only two matrices, as in a non-gated FFN.

questions.q: What is the key idea behind FlashAttention?
options: Approximating attention with low-rank projections
Dropping attention heads that contribute little
Quantizing Q and K to INT4
Tiling the computation in on-chip SRAM so the full n × n matrix is never written to HBM
questions.why: FlashAttention is IO-aware: it processes Q, K, V in blocks in fast on-chip memory and fuses softmax and matmuls, cutting slow memory traffic. It computes exact attention, unlike low-rank approximations such as Linformer.

questions.q: Which statement about FlashAttention is NOT true?
options: It produces approximate outputs that differ from standard attention
It reduces memory reads and writes to GPU HBM
It reduces activation memory for long sequences
It still performs O(n²) FLOPs
questions.why: FlashAttention computes exact attention (up to floating-point rounding); its gains come from memory traffic, not from skipping work. FLOPs are still quadratic, which is why D is a true statement and not the answer.

questions.q: Mistral 7B uses sliding-window attention with window w. What is the attention cost for a sequence of length n?
options: O(n²)
O(w²)
O(n · w)
O(log n)
questions.why: Each token attends only to the previous w tokens, so cost is linear in n for fixed w. Information can still travel further than w because each layer's window stacks over the previous layer's.

questions.q: Longformer handles long documents by combining which attention patterns?
options: Full attention in every layer with a larger head dimension
Random attention only
Local sliding-window attention plus a few global tokens that attend everywhere
Recurrence across chunks with no attention
questions.why: Most tokens attend within a local window, while designated global tokens (such as [CLS]) attend to and from all positions, giving linear scaling with task-relevant long-range links. Recurrence across chunks is the Transformer-XL approach.

questions.q: Mixtral 8x7B routes each token to the top 2 of 8 experts per layer. Which statement about its size is correct?
options: ≈ 47B total parameters but only ≈ 13B active per token
56B total and 56B active per token
7B total because experts share weights
14B total and 7B active per token
questions.why: Only the FFN experts are replicated (attention and embeddings are shared), so the total is ≈ 46.7B rather than 8 × 7 = 56B. With top-2 routing each token uses ≈ 12.9B parameters, giving roughly 13B-class compute per token.

questions.q: Why do MoE models add an auxiliary load-balancing loss?
options: To make all experts learn identical functions
To reduce the vocabulary size
To replace the language modeling loss
To stop the router from sending most tokens to a few experts while others go unused
questions.why: Routers tend to collapse onto favored experts, wasting capacity and overloading some devices. The auxiliary loss encourages an even token distribution; it is added to, not substituted for, the main loss.

questions.q: What is the main practical downside of an MoE model compared with a dense model of the same per-token compute?
options: It cannot use attention
All experts' weights must be held in memory even though only a few are used per token
It cannot be trained with backpropagation
It requires an encoder–decoder structure
questions.why: Any token may route to any expert, so the full parameter set must be resident, making memory needs closer to a much larger dense model. MoE routers are trained with ordinary backprop through the gate weights.

questions.q: Following the Chinchilla rule of thumb, roughly how many training tokens are compute-optimal for a 70B-parameter model?
questions.why: 70B × 20 tokens/parameter = 1.4T tokens, which is exactly what Chinchilla (70B) was trained on. 300B is roughly what the 175B GPT-3 used, illustrating its undertraining.

questions.q: Using C ≈ 6·N·D, how many FLOPs are needed to train a 1B-parameter model on 20B tokens?
questions.why: 6 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10¹⁰ = 1.2 × 10²⁰ FLOPs. The factor 6 comes from about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token in the forward pass and about 4 in the backward pass.

questions.q: How did the Chinchilla findings differ from the earlier Kaplan et al. (2020) scaling recommendations?
options: Kaplan favored growing parameters much faster than data; Chinchilla found parameters and tokens should grow roughly equally
Kaplan found data mattered more than parameters; Chinchilla reversed this
Chinchilla found loss is independent of dataset size
Chinchilla showed scaling laws do not apply to transformers
questions.why: Kaplan's fits led to very large models trained on relatively few tokens (like GPT-3). Chinchilla, with better learning-rate schedules per run, showed a smaller model trained on more tokens beats a larger undertrained one at equal compute.

questions.q: LLaMA trained a 7B model on 1T tokens, far more than Chinchilla-optimal. What is the main justification?
options: Chinchilla's results apply only to encoder models
More tokens reduce training compute
A smaller model trained longer is cheaper to serve at inference for a given quality
Larger datasets eliminate the need for attention
questions.why: Chinchilla optimizes training compute only; if a model will serve many requests, spending extra training compute to get a smaller model with the same quality pays off. Training longer increases, not reduces, training compute.

questions.q: In the decoder of an encoder–decoder transformer, where do the cross-attention queries, keys and values come from?
options: All three from the encoder output
Queries from the encoder, keys and values from the decoder
Queries from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder output
All three from the decoder's previous layer
questions.why: The decoder asks questions (queries) about the source sentence, which is represented by the encoder's keys and values. Swapping the roles (option B) would make the encoder states query the partial output, which is not how the decoder reads the source.

questions.q: How many attention sublayers does each decoder block in the original encoder–decoder transformer have?
options: Two: masked self-attention and cross-attention
One: masked self-attention only
Three: self-attention, cross-attention and global attention
None; it uses only feed-forward layers
questions.why: Each decoder block has masked self-attention over the output so far, cross-attention to the encoder, and then an FFN. A decoder-only GPT block has just the one masked self-attention sublayer.

questions.q: For sentence classification with BERT, which representation is typically fed to the classification head?
options: The embedding of the last token
The average of the input embeddings before any layer
The attention weights of the first head
The final hidden state of the [CLS] token
questions.why: BERT prepends [CLS], and because attention is bidirectional its final state aggregates the whole sequence. Using the last token's state is the convention for decoder-only models, where only the last position has seen everything.

questions.q: Why is a vanilla BERT model a poor choice for open-ended text generation?
options: Its vocabulary is too small
It is trained bidirectionally to fill masked tokens, not to predict the next token left to right
It has no attention layers
It cannot process more than 64 tokens
questions.why: BERT's representations assume access to both left and right context, which does not exist during generation. Its limit is 512 positions, not 64, and its 30K WordPiece vocabulary is not the obstacle.

questions.q: A team needs low-latency sentence embeddings for semantic search over millions of documents. Which architecture is the most efficient fit?
options: A large decoder-only chat model
A compact encoder-only model with pooled outputs
A diffusion model
An encoder–decoder translation model
questions.why: Encoder models like BERT-style sentence transformers produce one bidirectional vector per text in a single pass and are small enough to embed large corpora quickly. A large chat model can produce embeddings but is far slower and costlier per document.

questions.q: When training a causal LM on input token IDs [t₀, t₁, t₂, t₃], what are the targets?
options: The same sequence [t₀, t₁, t₂, t₃] at the same positions
A single class label for the whole sequence
Random masked positions only
The sequence shifted left by one: position i predicts tᵢ₊₁
questions.why: Logits at position i are compared with the token at i + 1, so every position provides a training signal in one pass. Predicting the same position would be trivial copying, and random masked positions describe BERT's MLM.

questions.q: A developer creates `nn.MultiheadAttention(embed_dim=512, num_heads=8)` with default arguments and passes a tensor of shape (32, 100, 512) meant as (batch, seq, embed). What goes wrong?
options: By default it expects (seq, batch, embed), so the batch and sequence axes are misread
It raises an error because 512 is not divisible by 8
It automatically applies a causal mask
Nothing; it always expects batch first
questions.why: `batch_first` defaults to False, so the 32 is treated as sequence length and 100 as batch, silently mixing information across examples. 512 / 8 = 64 is valid, and no causal mask is applied unless given.

questions.q: What does `is_causal=True` do in `torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)`?
options: Drops attention weights below a threshold
Masks padding tokens using the attention mask
Applies a lower-triangular mask so each query attends only to current and earlier keys
Enables dropout on the attention weights
questions.why: The flag builds the causal mask internally and lets PyTorch pick a fused kernel such as FlashAttention. Padding requires a separate `attn_mask`, and dropout is controlled by `dropout_p`.

questions.q:
Which normalization layout does this forward pass implement?

```python
def forward(self, x):
    x = x + self.attn(self.ln1(x))
    x = x + self.mlp(self.ln2(x))
    return x
```
options: Pre-norm
Post-norm
No normalization on the residual branch
BatchNorm after each sublayer
questions.why: Normalization is applied to the input of each sublayer, and the residual stream itself is never normalized, which is pre-norm (as in GPT-2). Post-norm would be `x = self.ln1(x + self.attn(x))`.

questions.q: Why do pre-norm transformers add one extra LayerNorm/RMSNorm after the last block, before the LM head?
options: To apply the causal mask
Because the residual stream is never normalized inside the blocks, its scale can grow and must be normalized before projection to logits
To convert hidden states into token IDs
To combine the outputs of attention heads
questions.why: In pre-norm, each sublayer adds to the raw residual, so the final hidden state's magnitude grows with depth. A final norm stabilizes the input to the LM head; head outputs are combined by W_O inside each attention layer.

questions.q: What property of the LSTM lets gradients survive over long time spans better than in a vanilla RNN?
options: It uses ReLU in every gate
It processes the sequence in reverse
It has no recurrent connection
Its cell state is updated additively, controlled by a forget gate
questions.why: The cell state cₜ = fₜ ⊙ cₜ₋₁ + iₜ ⊙ c̃ₜ lets gradients flow back without repeated squashing when the forget gate stays near 1. LSTM gates use sigmoids, not ReLU.

questions.q: When training a seq2seq decoder, the ground-truth previous token is fed as input at each step instead of the model's own prediction. What is this called?
options: Beam search
Label smoothing
Curriculum learning
Teacher forcing
questions.why: Teacher forcing speeds and stabilizes training and, in transformers, allows all positions to be trained in parallel with a causal mask. Its downside is exposure bias: at inference the model must consume its own possibly wrong outputs.

questions.q: What did Bahdanau-style attention add to RNN encoder–decoders?
options: At each output step, the decoder computes a weighted combination of all encoder hidden states
A convolution over the source sentence
A second encoder running right to left only
Positional encodings for the decoder
questions.why: The decoder scores every encoder state against its own state, softmaxes the scores and uses the weighted context vector, removing the fixed-vector bottleneck. Bidirectional encoders were used alongside it, but the attention mechanism itself is the dynamic weighted context.

questions.q: A multi-head attention layer has d_model = 512 and Q, K, V and output projections that each include a bias. How many parameters does it have?
questions.why: Each projection is 512 × 512 + 512 = 262,656, and there are four, giving 1,050,624. The head count does not change the total because heads split the same d_model; 1,048,576 omits the biases.

questions.q: A model has d_model = 4,096, 32 query heads of dimension 128, and 8 key/value heads. What is the shape of the key projection matrix W_K?
questions.why: W_K maps the 4,096-dim hidden state to 8 KV heads × 128 = 1,024 dims. 4,096 × 4,096 would be standard MHA with 32 KV heads, and 4,096 × 128 would be MQA with a single KV head.

questions.q: A ViT processes a 224 × 224 image with 16 × 16 patches. How many patch tokens are produced (excluding the class token)?
questions.why: 224 / 16 = 14 patches per side, and 14 × 14 = 196; adding the [CLS] token gives 197. 14 is only one side, and 3,136 would correspond to 4 × 4 patches (56 × 56).

questions.q: How does CLIP perform zero-shot image classification over a set of labels?
options: It fine-tunes a new classification head per label set
It generates a caption and parses the label from it
It retrieves similar labeled training images
It embeds prompts like "a photo of a {label}" and picks the label whose text embedding is most similar to the image embedding
questions.why: Because image and text share an embedding space, any label set can be turned into text prompts and compared by cosine similarity with no training. Fine-tuning a head is linear probing, which is not zero-shot.

questions.q: What makes latent diffusion models such as Stable Diffusion cheaper than pixel-space diffusion?
options: They use a GAN discriminator instead of denoising
They run the denoising process in a compressed latent space produced by a VAE encoder
They generate images in a single step
They skip the text conditioning
questions.why: A 512 × 512 × 3 image becomes a 64 × 64 × 4 latent, so every denoising step processes far fewer values, and the VAE decoder maps the final latent back to pixels. They still use many denoising steps unless a distilled sampler is used.

questions.q: In text-to-image diffusion, what does classifier-free guidance do?
options: Trains a separate image classifier to steer sampling
Extrapolates from the unconditional noise prediction toward the text-conditional prediction to strengthen prompt adherence
Removes the text encoder during sampling
Reduces the number of denoising steps to one
questions.why: The same model predicts noise with and without the prompt, and the output is ε_uncond + w·(ε_cond − ε_uncond). Using an external classifier's gradients is the older classifier guidance that CFG replaced.

questions.q: A team compares two image diffusion models and wants a metric of how close the distribution of generated images is to real images. Which metric is standard for this?
options: BLEU
Perplexity
Top-1 classification accuracy
Fréchet Inception Distance (FID)
questions.why: FID embeds real and generated images with an Inception network, fits a Gaussian to each set and computes the Fréchet distance between them; lower is better, and it reflects both quality and diversity. Perplexity needs tractable likelihoods and is not the standard way to compare image generators.

questions.q: Why do VAEs sample the latent as z = μ + σ ⊙ ε with ε ~ N(0, I)?
options: So gradients can flow through μ and σ despite the random sampling
To make the latent space discrete
To remove the KL term from the loss
To make the decoder deterministic at training time
questions.why: Sampling directly from N(μ, σ²) is not differentiable with respect to μ and σ, but moving the randomness into a fixed ε makes z a differentiable function of them. The KL term is still part of the loss.

questions.q: A batch contains sequences of different lengths padded to 128 tokens. Without a padding mask, what happens?
options: Training crashes with a shape error
The causal mask automatically ignores padding
Real tokens attend to pad tokens, so representations depend on how much padding was added
Pad tokens are removed by the tokenizer
questions.why: Pad positions get nonzero attention weight unless masked to −inf, contaminating outputs. A causal mask only blocks future positions, so it does not hide pads that precede real tokens (left padding) or any pads in a bidirectional encoder.

questions.q: Keeping d_model fixed, how does going from 8 to 16 attention heads affect the attention layer's parameters?
options: They double
They halve
They stay essentially the same, since each head's dimension halves
They grow quadratically
questions.why: With d_head = d_model / h, the Q, K, V and output projections are still d_model × d_model in total. More heads do create more (smaller) score matrices, so score memory grows even though parameters do not.

questions.q: `nn.MultiheadAttention(embed_dim=1000, num_heads=16)` raises an error. Why?
options: embed_dim must be a power of 2
embed_dim must be divisible by num_heads
num_heads must be at most 12
embed_dim must be smaller than the sequence length
questions.why: 1,000 / 16 = 62.5, so the embedding cannot be split evenly into per-head dimensions. Powers of 2 are common for hardware efficiency but are not required (e.g., 768 / 12 works).

questions.q: GPT-2 scales the initialization of residual-branch output projections by 1/√N, where N is the number of residual layers. What problem does this address?
options: The variance of the residual stream growing as more blocks add to it
Dying ReLU units
Too few attention heads
Tokens exceeding the vocabulary
questions.why: Each block adds its output to the residual stream, so variance accumulates with depth; shrinking those projections keeps the stream's scale stable at initialization. GELU-based GPT-2 does not suffer from dying ReLU.

questions.q: In the original transformer, where was dropout applied?
options: Only to the input token IDs
Only to the final logits
To each sublayer's output before the residual add, and to the summed embeddings and positional encodings
To the gradients during backpropagation
questions.why: Vaswani et al. applied residual dropout (rate 0.1 in the base model) to sublayer outputs and embeddings; many implementations also drop attention weights. Many modern large pretraining runs set dropout to 0 because one pass over huge data rarely overfits.

questions.q: If sequence length doubles from 4K to 8K tokens, how does the size of each layer's attention score matrix change?
options: It stays the same
It doubles
It grows 8×
It grows 4×
questions.why: The score matrix is n × n, so doubling n multiplies it by 2² = 4. The FFN cost and the per-token projections grow only linearly (2×).

questions.q: Why can a single transformer layer relate two tokens 1,000 positions apart while a CNN with 3-token kernels cannot?
options: CNNs use no weights
Self-attention connects every pair of positions directly, while a CNN's receptive field grows only a few tokens per layer
Transformers use larger embeddings
CNNs cannot process text
questions.why: Attention has a path length of 1 between any two tokens, whereas stacked 3-wide convolutions need hundreds of layers (or dilation) to span 1,000 tokens. CNNs can process text (e.g., ByteNet, TextCNN), so D is false.

questions.q: FlashAttention computes softmax over a row of scores without ever holding the full row in memory. What technique makes this possible?
options: Online softmax: keeping a running maximum and running normalizer per row and rescaling partial outputs as each new key block arrives
Replacing softmax with ReLU
Computing softmax only over the diagonal block
Precomputing softmax statistics from the previous training step
questions.why: When a new block raises the running max m, previous partial sums and outputs are multiplied by exp(m_old − m_new), so the final result equals the exact softmax. Replacing softmax or restricting to one block would change the output, but FlashAttention is exact.

questions.q: What is the extra memory complexity of FlashAttention's forward pass in sequence length n (beyond inputs and outputs)?
options: O(n²), same as standard attention
O(n), storing only per-row softmax statistics
O(n log n)
questions.why: FlashAttention saves the row max and log-sum-exp per query (O(n)) instead of the n × n probability matrix. These statistics are what make recomputation in the backward pass cheap.

questions.q: Which change is a key improvement of FlashAttention-2 over the original FlashAttention?
options: Switching from exact to approximate attention
Moving attention computation to the CPU
Fewer non-matmul FLOPs and parallelizing over the sequence-length dimension for better GPU occupancy
Storing the attention matrix in HBM for reuse
questions.why: FlashAttention-2 reduces rescaling work outside Tensor Core matmuls, splits work across thread blocks along the sequence as well as batch and heads, and partitions work better between warps. It remains exact and still avoids materializing the score matrix.

questions.q: Several long-context models increase RoPE's base (θ) from 10,000 to values such as 500,000. What effect does this have?
options: It lowers the rotation frequencies so positions far apart still map to distinguishable, not-yet-wrapped angles over a longer context
It increases the number of attention heads
It converts RoPE into absolute learned positions
It removes the need for a causal mask
questions.why: RoPE frequencies are θ^(−2i/d); a larger base stretches the wavelengths, especially of low-frequency dimensions, so longer distances are represented without angles the model never saw in training. It is a positional change only and does not affect head count or masking.

questions.q: To extend a RoPE model trained on 2K tokens to 8K, Position Interpolation (Chen et al., 2023) does what?
options: Trains new absolute position embeddings for positions 2K–8K
Uses sliding-window attention of 2K
Randomly drops 75% of tokens
Divides position indices by 4 so the 8K positions fall inside the trained 0–2K range, followed by brief fine-tuning
questions.why: Interpolating (scaling down) positions keeps rotation angles within the trained range, which proved far more stable than extrapolating to unseen angles. Sliding windows would limit, not extend, the effective attention span.

questions.q: Why is RoPE described as encoding *relative* position even though it rotates each vector by its absolute position?
options: It adds a learned bias per distance
It only applies to adjacent tokens
The dot product of a query rotated by m and a key rotated by n depends only on m − n
It normalizes positions by sequence length
questions.why: Rotations compose: (R_m q)·(R_n k) = q·(R_(n−m) k), so attention scores see only the offset. A learned bias per distance describes T5's relative position bias, a different method.

questions.q: How are ALiBi's per-head slopes chosen in a model with 8 heads?
options: Learned freely by gradient descent
A fixed geometric sequence (1/2, 1/4, …, 1/256), so different heads focus on different distance ranges
All heads use slope 1
Randomly sampled at each forward pass
questions.why: ALiBi uses non-learned head-specific slopes; steep slopes create local heads and shallow slopes allow long-range heads. A single shared slope would make all heads equally distance-biased.

questions.q: StreamingLLM observed that LLMs put disproportionately high attention on the first few tokens even when they are semantically unimportant. How does it exploit this to run with a rolling window?
options: It keeps the KV states of a few initial "sink" tokens alongside the most recent window
It deletes the first tokens to save memory
It retrains the model without a BOS token
It doubles the head dimension
questions.why: Softmax must put attention mass somewhere, and models learn to dump excess on initial tokens; evicting them in a plain sliding window makes perplexity blow up. Keeping a few sink tokens plus recent tokens restores stable streaming generation without retraining.

questions.q: What is the main efficiency advantage of state-space models such as Mamba over transformers for long sequences?
options: They use larger vocabularies
They have no trainable parameters
They require no GPU
Training scales linearly with sequence length and generation uses a fixed-size recurrent state instead of a growing cache
questions.why: An SSM compresses history into a constant-size state, so per-token generation cost and memory do not grow with context. The trade-off is that exact recall of arbitrary earlier tokens can be weaker than full attention.

questions.q: What does "selective" mean in Mamba's selective state-space layer?
options: Only some layers are trained
The SSM parameters (such as Δ, B and C) are functions of the current input, letting the model choose what to keep or forget
The model selects a subset of experts per token
Tokens are selected by top-k attention
questions.why: Earlier SSMs (like S4) used fixed, time-invariant parameters; Mamba makes them input-dependent, giving content-based gating similar to an RNN gate. Selecting experts per token describes MoE.

questions.q: Mamba's input-dependent parameters prevent computing the SSM as one global convolution. How does it still train efficiently on GPUs?
options: It trains one token at a time like a classic RNN
It falls back to full attention during training
It uses a hardware-aware parallel scan kept in fast on-chip memory
It approximates the recurrence with dropout
questions.why: The linear recurrence is associative, so it can be computed with a parallel (prefix) scan, and Mamba fuses this in SRAM to avoid materializing the expanded state in HBM. Time-invariant SSMs like S4 could use convolutions, but selectivity rules that out.

questions.q: Jamba combines which building blocks in one model?
options: Transformer attention layers, Mamba layers and MoE feed-forward layers
LSTMs and CNNs only
A diffusion decoder and a GAN discriminator
Encoder-only and encoder–decoder stacks
questions.why: Jamba interleaves a few attention layers among many Mamba layers, getting most of the memory efficiency of SSMs while keeping attention's precise recall, and adds MoE for capacity. Hybrids are a common answer to SSMs' weaker in-context retrieval.

questions.q: In MoE training, each expert has a capacity of (tokens per batch / number of experts) × capacity factor. What happens to tokens routed to an expert that is already full?
options: They are routed to every expert
The batch is discarded
They are typically dropped from that layer's expert computation and pass through via the residual connection
The expert's capacity automatically grows
questions.why: Fixed capacity gives static tensor shapes for efficient parallel execution, at the cost of "overflow" tokens skipping the expert. A higher capacity factor drops fewer tokens but wastes compute and memory on padding.

questions.q: How does the Switch Transformer simplify MoE routing compared with earlier top-2 designs?
options: It uses no router and averages all experts
It routes by token position
It routes each token to its top 4 experts
It routes each token to only its single top expert (top-1)
questions.why: Top-1 routing halves expert compute and communication compared with top-2 and simplifies implementation, and the paper showed it still works well with a load-balancing loss. Mixtral and many later models went back to top-2.

questions.q: DeepSeekMoE modifies standard MoE in which way?
options: It removes the router
It splits experts into many smaller ones and adds always-active shared experts for common knowledge
It routes at the sequence level rather than per token
It applies experts to attention heads only
questions.why: Fine-grained segmentation allows more flexible combinations of specialists, while shared experts absorb knowledge every token needs so routed experts can specialize. Routing is still per token through a learned gate.

questions.q: Xiong et al. (2020) analyzed why post-LN transformers need learning-rate warmup. What did they find?
options: At initialization, gradients near the output layers are large, so a full learning rate early on destabilizes training; pre-LN gradients are well-behaved
Post-LN has vanishing gradients only in the embedding layer
Warmup is needed only because of dropout
Pre-LN requires longer warmup than post-LN
questions.why: Their mean-field analysis showed post-LN's expected gradients at the last layers are large at init, while pre-LN gradients stay bounded, allowing training with little or no warmup. That is the opposite of option D.

questions.q: Large transformers sometimes diverge because attention logits grow very large, making softmax nearly one-hot. Which architectural fix targets this directly?
options: Removing the √d_k scaling
Adding more attention heads
Applying LayerNorm/RMSNorm to queries and keys before their dot product (QK-norm)
Using sigmoid in the FFN
questions.why: Normalizing Q and K bounds the magnitude of their dot products, preventing attention entropy collapse; it was used to stabilize ViT-22B and appears in several later LLMs. Removing the √d_k scaling would make logits larger, not smaller.

questions.q: Gemma 2 applies "soft-capping" to attention and final logits. What does it compute?
options: It clips logits to a hard maximum value
It divides logits by sequence length
It adds Gaussian noise to logits
cap · tanh(logits / cap), smoothly bounding logits to (−cap, cap)
questions.why: The tanh keeps small logits nearly unchanged while smoothly limiting extreme ones, improving stability without the zero gradient of a hard clip. Hard clipping (option A) would stop gradients for capped values.

questions.q: What is the purpose of μP (Maximal Update Parametrization)?
options: To quantize weights for inference
To parametrize initialization and per-layer learning rates so hyperparameters tuned on a narrow model transfer to a much wider one
To prune attention heads
To compute scaling laws for dataset size
questions.why: Under standard parametrization the optimal learning rate shifts with width, but μP scales things so it stays roughly constant ("μTransfer"). Teams can then tune on small proxies and train the large model once.

questions.q: Chinchilla fits loss as L(N, D) = E + A/N^α + B/D^β. What does the constant E represent?
options: The irreducible loss (entropy of natural text) that no model size or data amount removes
The loss of a model with zero parameters
The training compute budget
The embedding dimension
questions.why: As N and D grow, the two power-law terms shrink toward zero and loss approaches E. The finite-N and finite-D terms capture the model-size and data limitations respectively.

questions.q: Under Chinchilla-optimal scaling, if the training compute budget increases 10×, roughly how should model size and token count change?
options: Parameters 10×, tokens unchanged
Tokens 10×, parameters unchanged
Each about 3.2× (√10)
Each about 10×
questions.why: Since C ≈ 6ND and the optimal N and D scale roughly equally (each ∝ C^0.5), both grow by √10 ≈ 3.16. Growing both 10× would need 100× compute.

questions.q: Ignoring attention over the context, about how many FLOPs does a forward pass of an N-parameter decoder need per generated token?
options: N
6N
N²
2N
questions.why: Each parameter takes part in one multiply and one add per token, so the forward pass costs about 2N FLOPs; a 7B model needs ~14 GFLOPs per token. 6N is the training cost per token including the backward pass.

questions.q: Kaplan et al. note the forward pass costs about 2N + 2·n_layer·n_ctx·d_model FLOPs per token. When does the context-dependent attention term become significant compared with 2N?
options: When n_ctx is comparable to or larger than about 12·d_model
Whenever n_ctx exceeds the number of heads
Only when the model uses MoE
Never; it is always negligible
questions.why: With N ≈ 12·n_layer·d_model², the ratio of the attention term to 2N is n_ctx / (12·d_model). For d_model = 4,096 that threshold is ~49K tokens, which is why long-context training shifts the cost balance toward attention.

questions.q: Linear attention variants replace softmax(QKᵀ)V with φ(Q)(φ(K)ᵀV). Why does this reduce complexity to O(n)?
options: It reduces the number of heads to one
Matrix multiplication is associative, so φ(K)ᵀV (a d × d matrix) is computed first, avoiding the n × n matrix
It uses sparse attention patterns
It skips the value projection
questions.why: Without the softmax's row-wise normalization over QKᵀ, the product can be reordered so cost is O(n·d²) instead of O(n²·d). The kernel feature map φ only approximates softmax, so quality often lags full attention.

questions.q: DeepSeek-V2's Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) reduces inference memory in which way?
options: By sharing one KV head across all queries, as in MQA
By using sliding-window attention
By jointly compressing keys and values into a low-rank latent vector that is cached and projected back up per head
By storing attention scores instead of keys and values
questions.why: MLA caches a small latent per token and reconstructs per-head K and V with up-projections (which can be absorbed into other matrices), keeping per-head diversity unlike MQA. RoPE is handled with a separate decoupled key component because rotation does not commute with the compression.

questions.q: Mechanistic interpretability research describes "induction heads." What do they do?
options: Attend only to the BOS token
Implement the causal mask
Normalize the residual stream
Find an earlier occurrence of the current token and predict the token that followed it ([A][B] … [A] → [B])
questions.why: Induction heads arise from a two-layer circuit (a previous-token head plus a matching head) and appear abruptly during training alongside a jump in in-context learning ability. Masking is a fixed operation, not a learned head behavior.

questions.q: Why are individual neurons in LLMs often "polysemantic," responding to several unrelated concepts?
options: Because of the causal mask
The model represents more features than it has dimensions by storing them in superposition across overlapping directions
Because of weight tying
Because LayerNorm forces all neurons to be equal
questions.why: Sparse features can share dimensions with limited interference, so concepts are not aligned with single neurons. Sparse autoencoders are used to decompose activations into more interpretable, monosemantic features.

questions.q: What attention mask does a prefix language model (as used in some T5/UL2 configurations) apply?
options: Bidirectional attention within the prefix (input) and causal attention over the generated part
Fully bidirectional attention everywhere
Causal attention everywhere including the prefix
No attention within the prefix
questions.why: A prefix LM is decoder-only in structure but lets the conditioning text see itself fully, like an encoder, while keeping generation autoregressive. Fully causal attention (option C) is the standard GPT setup.

questions.q: GPT-J and PaLM use a "parallel" block, y = x + Attn(Norm(x)) + MLP(Norm(x)). What is the main motivation?
options: It removes the need for residual connections
It makes attention bidirectional
The attention and MLP input projections can be fused, speeding up training at large scale with little quality loss
It halves the number of parameters
questions.why: Because both branches read the same normalized input, their matmuls can be combined, and PaLM reported roughly 15% faster training. Parameter count is unchanged, since the same attention and MLP weights are still present.

questions.q: In DDPM, how can a noisy sample x_t be obtained from clean data x₀ in one step?
options: x_t = x₀ + t · ε
x_t = x₀ · ε^t
x_t is only reachable by applying t sequential noise steps
x_t = √ᾱ_t · x₀ + √(1 − ᾱ_t) · ε, with ε ~ N(0, I)
questions.why: Because Gaussian noise steps compose, any timestep has a closed form where ᾱ_t is the cumulative product of (1 − β_s). This lets training sample random timesteps directly instead of simulating the chain, which is why C is wrong.

questions.q: What does DDIM sampling offer for a diffusion model trained with the DDPM objective?
options: Deterministic sampling that can use far fewer steps without retraining the model
A new training objective that replaces noise prediction
A discriminator to sharpen images
Pixel-space generation instead of latent
questions.why: DDIM defines a non-Markovian reverse process consistent with the same training objective, so an existing noise-prediction network can sample in ~50 steps instead of 1,000. With zero stochasticity, the same starting noise always yields the same image.

questions.q: What does a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) change in the latent diffusion recipe?
options: It removes the VAE and denoises raw pixels only
It replaces the U-Net denoiser with a transformer operating on patches of the latent
It replaces diffusion with autoregressive decoding
It uses an LSTM for text conditioning
questions.why: DiT patchifies the latent like a ViT and conditions on timestep and class via adaptive layer norm, showing quality improves predictably with transformer compute. It still works in a VAE latent space and still uses iterative denoising.

questions.q: Why did the original ViT underperform comparable CNNs when trained only on ImageNet-1k, but outperform them after pretraining on much larger datasets?
options: ViT cannot process color images
ViT has more convolutional layers
ViT lacks CNNs' built-in locality and translation-equivariance biases, so it needs more data to learn them
ViT uses a smaller patch size than CNN kernels
questions.why: Weaker inductive biases hurt with limited data but stop mattering, and even help, at scale. Later work such as DeiT used strong augmentation and distillation to train ViTs well on ImageNet alone.

questions.q: How is CLIP's training loss computed for a batch of N image–text pairs?
options: Mean squared error between image and text embeddings
A GAN loss on generated captions
Next-token cross-entropy on the captions only
Symmetric cross-entropy over the N × N similarity matrix, with matching pairs on the diagonal as the targets, using a learned temperature
questions.why: Each image must pick its caption among N texts and vice versa, so the other N − 1 items act as negatives, which is why very large batches help. MSE alone would pull embeddings together without pushing mismatched pairs apart, inviting collapse.

questions.q: In LLaVA-style multimodal LLMs, how are images fed into the language model?
options: A pretrained vision encoder (e.g., CLIP ViT) produces patch features, which a projector maps into the LLM's token embedding space
Images are converted to text captions by OCR before the LLM sees them
Pixels are tokenized with the text BPE vocabulary
The LLM's attention layers are replaced with convolutions
questions.why: The projected visual tokens are placed in the input sequence alongside text tokens, so the unchanged LLM attends to them. Captioning first would discard most visual detail.

questions.q: Standard attention stores the n × n probability matrix for the backward pass. What does FlashAttention do instead?
options: It skips gradients for attention entirely
It recomputes attention blocks in the backward pass from Q, K, V and the saved softmax statistics
It stores the matrix on the CPU
It uses the forward attention weights from the previous step
questions.why: Recomputation adds FLOPs but avoids reading a huge matrix from HBM, so the backward pass is still faster overall, since attention is memory-bound. Offloading to the CPU would be far slower.

questions.q: The GQA paper converts an existing multi-head attention checkpoint into a grouped-query model. How?
options: By retraining the model from scratch
By keeping only the first KV head of each group
By mean-pooling the key and value projection heads within each group, then uptraining on a small fraction of the original compute
By concatenating all KV heads into one
questions.why: Ainslie et al. found mean-pooling preserved more information than picking a single head, and about 5% of the pretraining compute recovered quality close to MHA. Training from scratch would work but defeats the purpose of reusing the checkpoint.

questions.q: A 32-layer model uses sliding-window attention with window 4,096. What is the theoretical maximum distance information can travel from input to the top layer?
options: 4,096 tokens
8,192 tokens
32 tokens
About 131K tokens (32 × 4,096)
questions.why: Each layer lets information move up to one window further back, so the receptive field grows roughly linearly with depth, like stacked convolutions; Mistral 7B cites ~131K. In practice information decays over many hops, so effective long-range recall is weaker than this bound.
